title: Synchronizers for asynchronous rounds
summary: Understand how a synchronizer makes an asynchronous system safe to run a synchronous round-based algorithm.
objectives: Explain what the α synchronizer removes and adds

sourceLens.whyExaminable: A synchronizer is the bridge between asynchronous message passing and a synchronous round algorithm. The key question is when a process is safe to advance.

sections.title: Safe to proceed
sections.body: In an asynchronous system, a synchronizer tells a process when it is safe to move to the next simulated synchronous round. Safety means that the messages and acknowledgements required by the current round have been accounted for.

sections.title: Simple and α synchronizers
sections.body: The simple synchronizer assumes every process sends exactly one message to every neighbor per round, using a dummy message when necessary. The α synchronizer removes that fixed-message assumption and must therefore reason about when all current-round communication is complete.

math.name: Safe-to-proceed condition
math.purpose: State the condition that allows a process to advance to the next simulated round.
math.explanation: A process advances only after the synchronizer has evidence that the current-round communication required by its protocol is complete.

examples.title: Round barrier reasoning
steps: Track messages sent for that round.
Track acknowledgements or safe notifications from neighbors.
Advance only when the protocol's safety condition holds.
examples.answer: A synchronizer is a correctness mechanism: it creates a round barrier without assuming that the underlying network is synchronous.

examples.title: Dummy message versus alpha completion
steps: In the simple synchronizer, process $p$ expects one current-round message from neighbors $q$ and $r$.
If $p$ has no payload for $q$, it sends a dummy message so the edge still has one completion signal.
After the expected messages or acknowledgements arrive, $p$ can satisfy the round-barrier condition.
In the $\alpha$ synchronizer, the fixed count is removed, so $p$ needs safe notifications that all current-round communication is complete.
examples.answer: The dummy message makes the simple protocol's fixed-count assumption observable; $\alpha$ replaces that shortcut with explicit completion evidence.

contrastDrills.prompt: What does a synchronizer add to an asynchronous system?
choices: A safe-to-proceed rule for simulated rounds
contrastDrills.explanation: A synchronizer supplies the protocol condition for advancing a simulated synchronous round; it does not make the physical system synchronous.
contrastDrills.misconception: Logical round coordination is not the same as synchronized wall clocks.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why can a dummy message be useful in the simple synchronizer?
criticalQuestions.angle: Consider how the protocol knows that a process has finished its current round.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The dummy message preserves the one-message-per-neighbor assumption, so receipt of a message still signals completion of that neighbor's current-round communication even when there is no payload.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What assumption does the $\alpha$ synchronizer remove, and what new evidence must it track?
criticalQuestions.angle: Compare fixed message counts with protocol evidence about completion of current-round communication.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The $\alpha$ synchronizer removes the assumption that every process sends exactly one message to every neighbor per round. It must instead track enough acknowledgements or safe notifications to establish that current-round communication is complete before advancing.
